result: SARS-CoV-2 has infected approximately 10% of the world's population and killed a confirmed ~5 million people, but likely considerably more.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 present epidemiological statistics about SARS-CoV-2 infection and mortality rates. These are presented as background knowledge without supporting data or citations in the manuscript itself, making them uncertain in the context of this work's original contributions.

result: Multiple factors including vaccine distribution inequities, waning immunity, and viral variants challenge pandemic containment.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5 are supported by citations to published literature (Diamond et al., 2021; Lavine et al., 2021; Fraser et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b) discussing these challenges to pandemic containment.

result: The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein is the major surface glycoprotein that mediates viral entry by binding ACE2 and triggering membrane fusion, existing as a homotrimer with S1 and S2 domains.
evaluation: Claims C6-C11 describe established structural and functional properties of the spike protein, supported by multiple citations to published literature (Zhou et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020; Li et al., 2003; Li, 2016; Letko et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020).

result: The RBD has been the major target of immunotherapeutics, but RBD point mutants have evolved to bypass neutralizing antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by citations to published literature on immunotherapeutics and viral escape (Hartenian et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Baum et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021b; Liu et al., 2021a; Weisblum et al., 2020; Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Starr et al., 2021).

result: Nanobodies possess multiple advantages over conventional antibodies including small size (~15 kDa), high affinity, stability, ease of production, low immunogenicity, and potential for nebulized delivery to the lungs.
evaluation: Claims C14-C22 describe established properties of nanobodies, supported by citations to published literature (Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020; Muyldermans, 2013; Corti et al., 2021; Revets et al., 2005; Bannas et al., 2017; Chanier and Chames, 2019; Vincke et al., 2009; Duggan, 2018; Wölfel et al., 2020; Nambulli et al., 2021; Erreni et al., 2020; Van Heeke et al., 2017; Zare et al., 2021).

result: 453 nanobodies are available against SARS-CoV-2 spike, primarily recognizing RBD regions with many subject to escape variation.
evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by citations to published literature on available nanobodies (Niu et al., 2021; Raybould et al., 2021; Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021; Huo et al., 2020a; Pymm et al., 2021; Hanke et al., 2020; Custódio et al., 2020; Esparza et al., 2020; Wrapp, 2020a; Dong et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021).

result: The authors generated a large, diverse repertoire of 116 high-quality nanobodies against SARS-CoV-2 spike by optimizing their generation pipeline, using affinity purification, LC-MS/MS analysis, and CDR3 clustering to maximize diversity.
evaluation: Claims C25-C41 describe the nanobody generation methodology and results, supported by Figure 1A-C and detailed methods. The clustering analysis showed minimal overlap between S1 and S2 nanobodies (4/183 clusters), diverse CDR3 lengths (3-22 amino acids), and limited overlap with other published repertoires (1/109 clusters shared with Xiang et al., 2020), demonstrating successful generation of a diverse repertoire.

result: All 116 nanobodies bound with high affinity (>60% with KD < 1 nM, two with picomolar affinities), with 71 binding RBD, 19 binding non-RBD S1, and 26 binding S2, showing fast association rates (many kon ≥ 10^6) that surpass high-performing monoclonal antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C42-C51 are supported by SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1-2. The distribution across spike domains and kinetic properties are well-documented. The lower number of non-RBD and S2 nanobodies is reasonably attributed to glycan shielding (C47), supported by citations (Grant et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).

result: Six of seven tested nanobodies retained strong binding to B.1.1.7/alpha and B.1.351/beta variants, with S1-23 showing reduced binding to alpha (17 pM to 230 pM) and abolished binding to beta, primarily through effects on off rates.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by SPR data in Figure 2G and Table 3. The variant binding data demonstrate that most nanobodies maintain activity against variants, with quantitative KD measurements provided. The observation that off rates are most affected is supported by citations (VanCott et al., 1994; Magnus, 2013; Steckbeck et al., 2005).

result: Nanobodies exhibit thermal stability (Tm 50-80°C) and maintain stability, kinetics, and affinity after freeze-drying without cryoprotectants.
evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by DSF data and lyophilization experiments shown in Figure 2D-F. The thermal stability range is consistent with published nanobody properties (Muyldermans, 2013), and the lyophilization data demonstrate practical stability for therapeutic applications.

result: Epitope mapping revealed three large, mostly non-overlapping bins for anti-RBD nanobodies (with at least eight sub-bins by gap statistic), four S1-non-RBD bins, five S2 bins, and demonstrated that at least three different nanobodies can bind simultaneously to the RBD.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by biolayer interferometry data in Figure 3A-C, gap statistic analysis (Tibshirani et al., 2001), and mass photometry data in Figure 3G. The simultaneous binding of three nanobodies to RBD contrasts with larger immunoglobulins and is supported by citations (Corti et al., 2021; Stewart et al., 1997; Xu et al., 2021).

result: 36% of monomeric nanobodies neutralized with IC50s ≤100 nM (23% <50 nM, 17 at ≤20 nM), with the most potent mapping to RBD, but importantly, nanobodies binding outside the RBD also showed neutralizing activity, representing the first evidence of nanobody neutralization outside the RBD.
evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are supported by pseudovirus neutralization data in Figure 4A-C. The neutralization of non-RBD binding nanobodies (e.g., S1-64, S1-65) is novel and well-documented. The claim of being 'first evidence' (C69) is a strong statement but appears justified given the literature review presented.

result: Oligomerization significantly improved IC50s and affinities for most nanobodies, with dramatic improvements observed (e.g., S1-RBD-35: ~12 nM to ~70 pM for trimer; S2-7: non-neutralizer to ~30 nM for tetramer), though enhancement was not universal and must be determined empirically.
evaluation: Claims C70-C75 are supported by oligomerization data in Figure 4D-F and Table 4. The quantitative improvements are well-documented, and the caveat that enhancement is not universal (C75) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

result: Seven of 27 tested anti-RBD nanobodies neutralized SARS-CoV-1 pseudovirus, with S1-1, S1-39, and S1-RBD-6 showing similar IC50s against both SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-1, while S1-23, S1-37, and S1-48 showed no activity against SARS-CoV-1. Additionally, 3 of 11 non-RBD nanobodies neutralized SARS-CoV-1.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by SARS-CoV-1 pseudovirus neutralization data in Figure 4K and Table 5. The cross-neutralization data are well-documented and demonstrate the breadth of the nanobody repertoire.

result: All tested nanobodies that neutralized pseudovirus also showed potent neutralization of authentic SARS-CoV-2 in plaque/focus reduction assays and in primary human airway epithelial cell (ALI) cultures, with S1-1 showing potent neutralization and S1-23 showing dose-dependent inhibition that was enhanced as a trimer.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by authentic virus neutralization data in Figure 5A and Table 6, and ALI culture data in Figure 5C. The correlation between pseudovirus and authentic virus assays validates the pseudovirus screening approach, and the ALI culture data demonstrate efficacy in a physiologically relevant model.

result: 32 unique escape mutants were identified against 22 nanobodies, with some selecting mutations at positions known from human antibody studies (e.g., E484K) and others selecting novel mutations. Importantly, combining two nanobodies in cocktails prevented escape in 8/9 cases, elevating the genetic barrier by requiring multiple mutations.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 are supported by escape mutant selection data in Table 7 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E. The cocktail data demonstrate a critical advantage for therapeutic development. However, the interpretation that 'simply combining two nanobodies imposed the requirement for a minimum of two amino acid substitutions' (C88) is somewhat inferential, though well-supported by the data.

result: Using integrative modeling with IMP, the authors solved structures for 21 neutralizing nanobodies (18 RBD, 1 NTD, 2 S2) classified into 10 groups, showing that neutralizing nanobodies bind at sites complementary to glycosylation sites and are concentrated at the glycan-free RBD.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by integrative modeling data in Figure 6, with spatial restraints from escape mutant data (Table 7) and cross-linking MS (Table 8). The modeling approach is validated by benchmarking against a published structure (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). However, the models provide moderate resolution and the authors appropriately note that higher-resolution studies are warranted.

result: Among the entire repertoire, ~80% of anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing, ~20% of anti-S2 nanobodies are neutralizing, and ~60% of non-RBD anti-S1 nanobodies are neutralizing, with the repertoire exploring much of the remaining available epitope space given glycosylation constraints.
evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by neutralization data across Figures 3, 4, and 6, with epitope mapping showing concentration on the RBD. The interpretation that the repertoire explores much of the available epitope space (C97) is reasonable given glycosylation constraints cited (Watanabe et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).

result: The authors present the first neutralizing nanobodies that bind to S2 (groups 9 and 10).
evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by data in Figures 2, 4, 6, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. This represents a novel finding, as S2-targeting nanobodies with neutralizing activity have not been previously reported. The structural mapping provides mechanistic insights into their function.

result: Powerfully synergistic effects were observed between numerous nanobody pairs, with dramatic potency increases: S1-23+S1-1 (~32- and ~21-fold), S1-RBD-15+S1-23 (~300-fold for S1-23), S1-49+S1-1 (>1000-fold), and S2-10-dimer with S1-23 or S1-RBD-15 (>4000-fold).
evaluation: Claims C99-C104 are supported by synergy data in Figure 7 and Table 9, using multiple synergy models (MuSyC, equivalent dose, BRAID). The quantitative fold-changes are well-documented, and the structural basis for synergy is explained through epitope mapping and RBD conformational dynamics. The extraordinary synergy with S2-10-dimer is particularly notable.
